questions.question: What are the four essential sections of an Architecture Decision Record (ADR)?
questions.explanation: An ADR captures: Title (what is being decided), Context (the current situation and forces), Decision (what was chosen and why), and Consequences (both positive and negative outcomes of the decision).

questions.question: Why is the 'Consequences' section the most important part of an ADR?
choices: It's the longest section so it looks more thorough
It captures both positive and negative trade-offs, helping future teams understand what was sacrificed and why, preventing repeated debates
It's the only section that project managers read
Consequences are optional and rarely useful
questions.explanation: The consequences section is where the real value lies — it documents trade-offs explicitly. When future team members question a decision, the ADR explains not just what was chosen but what was given up, preventing the same debates from recurring.

questions.question: When should you write an ADR?
choices: Only when the CTO requests one
Whenever a significant technical decision is made that will affect the team or project long-term
After the project is completely finished
Only for decisions that turn out to be wrong
questions.explanation: ADRs should be written for significant, lasting technical decisions — database choice, architecture pattern, framework selection. The goal is to capture the reasoning while it's fresh, so future team members don't have to guess or re-debate.
